title: Population-Based Carrier Screening
summary: Expanded carrier screening, ACOG/ACMG guidelines, and equitable access to reproductive genomics.

content_blocks.text: Carrier screening identifies individuals who carry one copy of a pathogenic variant in an autosomal recessive condition — they are healthy but at risk of having an affected child if their partner is also a carrier. Traditional carrier screening was ethnicity-based (Ashkenazi Jewish panel, sickle cell for African Americans). Expanded carrier screening (ECS) tests for hundreds of recessive conditions regardless of ethnicity.

In 2023, ACOG and ACMG jointly updated recommendations to endorse ECS over ethnicity-based screening. The updated guidance recommends offering ECS to all patients preconception or in early pregnancy as the preferred approach. Conditions included in ECS panels must meet criteria: well-defined phenotype, significant morbidity/mortality, disease frequency >1/100,000, and available treatment or reproductive options.

content_blocks.label: Couples who are both carriers of the same recessive condition when ECS is performed
content_blocks.context: Among couples where both partners undergo ECS, approximately 1 in 4 are 'at-risk couples' with 25% chance of an affected pregnancy

concepts.definition: Proportion of the population carrying one pathogenic allele for a recessive condition — varies by ancestry and condition
Remaining carrier risk after a negative carrier screen — depends on detection rate of the panel for that variant/ancestry
Couple-based screens both partners simultaneously; sequential screens one first, then the partner only if first is positive
Genetic testing of IVF embryos before implantation — allows selection of unaffected embryos for at-risk couples
cfDNA-based screening for chromosomal aneuploidy (trisomy 21, 18, 13) and sex chromosomes from maternal blood at 10+ weeks
Fetal DNA fragments in maternal circulation — source material for NIPT

content_blocks.body: Expanded carrier screening panels cost $250–$600 out of pocket when not covered by insurance. Coverage varies dramatically by insurer and state. This creates equity gaps: well-insured, educated patients access ECS; underserved populations often do not. Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and Title X family planning programs are key access points for expanding ECS to underserved communities. Several states have mandated ECS insurance coverage.
